questions.question: What does a trunk link do?
choices: Connects a PC to a switch
questions.explanation: A trunk carries traffic for multiple VLANs between switches using 802.1Q.

correct.explanation: A trunk tags frames with 802.1Q VLAN IDs so multiple VLANs cross one inter-switch link.

incorrect.explanation: Access ports carry a single VLAN untagged — trunks carry many VLANs with tags.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Describing access-port behavior on a trunk question
incorrect.whatItDoes: Carries one VLAN only describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for trunk purpose.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given trunk purpose, Carries multiple VLANs between switches matches the tested behavior — Carries one VLAN only applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: PC-to-switch links are access ports — trunks connect switches (or switch to router-on-a-stick).
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Using end-host access link for trunk definition
incorrect.whatItDoes: Connects a PC to a switch describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for trunk purpose.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given trunk purpose, Carries multiple VLANs between switches matches the tested behavior — Connects a PC to a switch applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Routing between VLANs needs a Layer 3 device — trunks extend Layer 2 VLANs across links, not route them.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Expecting trunk to route between VLANs
incorrect.whatItDoes: Routes between VLANs describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for trunk purpose.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given trunk purpose, Carries multiple VLANs between switches matches the tested behavior — Routes between VLANs applies a different mechanism.

answerReview.examTip: Trunk = 802.1Q tags on inter-switch links; native VLAN must match both ends.

questions.question: How big is the 802.1Q tag added to a frame?
questions.explanation: The 802.1Q tag is 4 bytes and contains the 12-bit VLAN ID.

correct.explanation: The 802.1Q tag is 4 bytes and contains the 12-bit VLAN ID.

incorrect.explanation: 2 bytes uses the wrong value. The tested fact calls for 802 — not 2.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 2 bytes describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for tag size.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given tag size, 4 bytes matches the tested behavior — 2 bytes applies a different mechanism.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Memorizing 2 instead of the correct 802

incorrect.explanation: 8 bytes uses the wrong value. The tested fact calls for 802 — not 8.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 8 bytes describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for tag size.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given tag size, 4 bytes matches the tested behavior — 8 bytes applies a different mechanism.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Memorizing 8 instead of the correct 802

incorrect.explanation: 12 bytes uses the wrong value. The tested fact calls for 802 — not 12.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 12 bytes describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for tag size.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given tag size, 4 bytes matches the tested behavior — 12 bytes applies a different mechanism.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Memorizing 12 instead of the correct 802

answerReview.examTip: On the exam: A trunk is faster than an access port — A trunk simply carries multiple VLANs; speed depends on the physical link

questions.question: On an 802.1Q trunk, how is the native VLAN’s traffic sent?
questions.explanation: Native VLAN frames cross the trunk untagged.

correct.explanation: Native VLAN frames cross an 802.1Q trunk untagged — all other VLANs are tagged with their VLAN ID.

incorrect.explanation: Double-tagging (Q-in-Q) is a provider technique — standard native VLAN traffic is sent with no 802.1Q tag.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Applying Q-in-Q to standard native VLAN behavior
incorrect.whatItDoes: Double-tagged describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for native vlan.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given native vlan, Untagged matches the tested behavior — Double-tagged applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Tagged frames carry an 802.1Q header — only non-native VLANs are tagged on a trunk.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Tagging native VLAN traffic like all other VLANs
incorrect.whatItDoes: Tagged describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for native vlan.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given native vlan, Untagged matches the tested behavior — Tagged applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Native VLAN traffic is forwarded normally — it is not dropped for lacking a tag.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Assuming untagged native VLAN frames are discarded
incorrect.whatItDoes: Dropped implies the device should discard the frame instead of forwarding or flooding it.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given native vlan, Untagged matches the tested behavior — Dropped applies a different mechanism.

answerReview.examTip: Trunk rule: native VLAN = untagged; all others tagged. Match native VLAN both ends.

questions.question: Two trunked switches log a native VLAN mismatch. What is the likely effect?
choices: Traffic from those VLANs can leak/merge
questions.explanation: A native VLAN mismatch can merge the two native VLANs’ traffic and triggers a CDP warning.

correct.explanation: Native VLAN mismatch puts each switch's untagged traffic into the peer's native VLAN — traffic can leak between VLANs and CDP reports the error.

incorrect.explanation: Trunk speed is negotiated separately — native VLAN mismatch affects which VLAN receives untagged frames, not link speed.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Confusing VLAN mismatch with speed/duplex issues
incorrect.whatItDoes: Trunk speed drops implies the device should discard the frame instead of forwarding or flooding it.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given native mismatch, Traffic from those VLANs can leak/merge matches the tested behavior — Trunk speed drops applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Tagged VLANs still work on a mismatched native VLAN trunk — the problem is untagged traffic landing in the wrong VLAN, not a total trunk shutdown.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Expecting all VLANs to fail when only native is mismatched
incorrect.whatItDoes: All VLANs stop describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for native mismatch.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given native mismatch, Traffic from those VLANs can leak/merge matches the tested behavior — All VLANs stop applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: CDP logs %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH because the misconfiguration has real forwarding impact — it is not cosmetic.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Treating native VLAN mismatch as harmless warning
incorrect.whatItDoes: Nothing — it is cosmetic describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for native mismatch.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given native mismatch, Traffic from those VLANs can leak/merge matches the tested behavior — Nothing — it is cosmetic applies a different mechanism.

answerReview.examTip: Native VLAN mismatch → untagged traffic bleeds into wrong VLAN. Fix both ends.

questions.question: Which command forces a port to trunk?
questions.explanation: switchport mode trunk sets the port to trunking.

correct.explanation: switchport mode trunk forces the port to operate as an 802.1Q trunk regardless of DTP negotiation.

incorrect.explanation: switchport mode access keeps the port in access mode — it will not carry multiple VLANs as a trunk.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Selecting access mode when trunk is required
incorrect.whatItDoes: switchport mode access describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for config trunk.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given config trunk, switchport mode trunk matches the tested behavior — switchport mode access applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: switchport trunk allowed vlan filters which VLANs cross the trunk — it does not change the port to trunk mode by itself.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Believing allowed-VLAN command sets trunk mode
incorrect.whatItDoes: switchport trunk allowed vlan describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for config trunk.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given config trunk, switchport mode trunk matches the tested behavior — switchport trunk allowed vlan applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: switchport nonegotiate disables DTP but does not force trunk — you still need switchport mode trunk (or dynamic desirable/auto).
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Equating nonegotiate with forcing trunk mode
incorrect.whatItDoes: switchport nonegotiate describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for config trunk.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given config trunk, switchport mode trunk matches the tested behavior — switchport nonegotiate applies a different mechanism.

answerReview.examTip: Force trunk → switchport mode trunk (then tune allowed/native VLANs).

questions.question: Which command disables DTP auto-negotiation on a port?
questions.explanation: switchport nonegotiate stops DTP, a hardening best practice.

correct.explanation: switchport nonegotiate stops DTP from sending negotiation frames — the port stays in whatever mode you configured manually.

incorrect.explanation: no dtp is not standard IOS trunk syntax — DTP is disabled per interface with switchport nonegotiate.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Inventing global no dtp command
incorrect.whatItDoes: no dtp describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for DTP security.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given DTP security, switchport nonegotiate matches the tested behavior — no dtp applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: switchport mode dynamic participates in DTP negotiation — it does not disable auto-negotiation.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Using dynamic mode to stop DTP
incorrect.whatItDoes: switchport mode dynamic describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for DTP security.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given DTP security, switchport nonegotiate matches the tested behavior — switchport mode dynamic applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: no switchport trunk is not the command to disable DTP — use switchport nonegotiate on the interface.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Negating switchport trunk instead of nonegotiate
incorrect.whatItDoes: no switchport trunk describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for DTP security.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given DTP security, switchport nonegotiate matches the tested behavior — no switchport trunk applies a different mechanism.

answerReview.examTip: Disable DTP on a trunk → switchport nonegotiate after setting the mode.

questions.question: Which command shows trunk mode, native VLAN, and allowed VLANs?
questions.explanation: show interfaces trunk lists trunking details.

correct.explanation: show interfaces trunk lists trunking status, native VLAN, and allowed VLANs per trunk interface.

incorrect.explanation: show vlan brief lists VLAN IDs and port assignments — it does not show trunk encapsulation, native VLAN, or allowed lists.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Using VLAN brief for trunk operational detail
incorrect.whatItDoes: show vlan brief describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for verify trunk.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given verify trunk, show interfaces trunk matches the tested behavior — show vlan brief applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: show ip interface brief summarizes Layer 3 status — trunk mode and allowed VLANs are Layer 2 trunk parameters.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Checking IP brief for trunk VLAN details
incorrect.whatItDoes: show ip interface brief describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for verify trunk.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given verify trunk, show interfaces trunk matches the tested behavior — show ip interface brief applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: show cdp neighbors discovers adjacent devices — it does not report 802.1Q trunk configuration.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Using CDP neighbors for trunk verification
incorrect.whatItDoes: show cdp neighbors describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for verify trunk.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given verify trunk, show interfaces trunk matches the tested behavior — show cdp neighbors applies a different mechanism.

questions.question: Which command limits a trunk to VLANs 10 and 20?
questions.explanation: switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20 prunes the trunk.

correct.explanation: switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20 prunes the trunk.

incorrect.explanation: switchport access vlan 10,20 reflects a common trap: A trunk is faster than an access port. A trunk simply carries multiple VLANs; speed depends on the physical link.
incorrect.whatItDoes: switchport access vlan 10,20 describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for allowed vlans.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given allowed vlans, switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20 matches the tested behavior — switchport access vlan 10,20 applies a different mechanism.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: A trunk is faster than an access port

incorrect.explanation: vlan 10,20 uses the wrong value. The tested fact calls for 20 — not 10.
incorrect.whatItDoes: vlan 10,20 describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for allowed vlans.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given allowed vlans, switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20 matches the tested behavior — vlan 10,20 applies a different mechanism.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Memorizing 10 instead of the correct 20

incorrect.explanation: switchport trunk native vlan 10 reflects a common trap: A trunk is faster than an access port. A trunk simply carries multiple VLANs; speed depends on the physical link.
incorrect.whatItDoes: switchport trunk native vlan 10 describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for allowed vlans.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given allowed vlans, switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20 matches the tested behavior — switchport trunk native vlan 10 applies a different mechanism.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: A trunk is faster than an access port
